source.version: Journal version of record: Nature Human Behaviour, Volume 9, June 2025, pp. 1107–1109, Matters arising, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02173-x. Received 9 December 2024, accepted 12 March 2025, published online 14 May 2025. Arising from B. C. Lee & J. J. Chung, Nature Human Behaviour (2024), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-024-01953-1. The 10-page PDF holds the 3 article pages (PDF pp. 1-3) and the 7-page Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary (PDF pp. 4-10).
source.title_on_document: ChatGPT decreases idea diversity in brainstorming

supplement.where: Online with the article at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02173-x (Additional information, p. 1109, PDF p. 3); the file is https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41562-025-02173-x/MediaObjects/41562_2025_2173_MOESM1_ESM.pdf (8 pages, read at finalization; 'SI p.' locators refer to its pages). The scripts behind the main text and the Supplementary Information are at https://osf.io/zf3s2 (Code availability, p. 1109).
supplement.holds: Supplementary Table 1 (SI pp. 2-8), which the main text cites for the statistical comparisons between conditions (Fig. 1 legend, p. 1108) and for the robustness analyses with thresholds 0.75 and 0.85 and three alternative metrics, 45 comparisons of which 37 are significant (p. 1108). For each contrast it gives the n of each condition (for Experiment 5 only the total, n = 383), the unique-idea percentages at thresholds 0.80, 0.75 and 0.85 with the risk difference, a 95% CI, Cohen's h and a proportions z-test, and the centroid similarity, pairwise similarity and minimum-spanning-tree results (OLS t-tests; a permutation test). Its legend says the p-values are two-sided and Bonferroni corrected within each experiment; it does not say that the CIs are corrected. It has no test of ChatGPT-only versus Human-only in Experiment 2b. The main text prints no test statistic, p-value, interval bound, or per-condition count of people or ideas, except 96 ChatGPT-aided ideas in Experiment 2a. The Reporting Summary ticks 'Confirmed' for exact per-condition sample sizes, the statistical tests, and effect sizes (PDF p. 4).

paper_design_summary: A Matters Arising reanalysis of the public data of Lee and Chung (2024), whose experiments randomized participants to generate an idea for a creative challenge with or without ChatGPT (comparison arms: web search or no aid). For each condition's pool of ideas, the authors compute the fraction of unique idea concepts, where two ideas overlap when the cosine similarity of their Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings exceeds 0.8, and compare it across conditions in six panels (Experiments 1, 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 5). Experiment 2b adds a set of ideas generated by ChatGPT alone.

outcomes.name: Fraction of unique idea concepts in each condition's pool of ideas (threshold 0.8)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Unique fraction = number of unique idea concepts / total ideas in the condition's set. Two ideas overlap when the cosine similarity of their Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings exceeds 0.8; a unique concept is a group of one or more ideas that overlap with no other idea in the set. The count of unique concepts could also be read as category_count (clusters formed by thresholded similarity). Robustness variants, reported only in the Supplementary Information: thresholds 0.75 and 0.85; aggregated comparisons of similarity scores; pairwise comparisons of similarity scores; mean edge distance in minimum spanning trees (37 of 45 comparisons significant, p. 1108).

contrasts.reported: Unique fraction (Fig. 1 bar labels): Web-search-assisted 0.96 vs ChatGPT-assisted 0.74. Error bars are 95% CIs for individual proportions, not printed as numbers. Text: AI-aided sets are less diverse in all five experiments, significant in four of five comparisons, the non-significant one in experiment 4. Tests and Bonferroni-corrected CIs for differences are in Supplementary Table 1 (not in this PDF).
contrasts.locator: p. 1108 (PDF p. 2), Fig. 1 panel 'Experiment 1: web search versus ChatGPT ideas'; text, left column below Fig. 1

diversity_detail.metric: Fraction of unique idea concepts (unique concepts / total ideas); overlap = Universal Sentence Encoder cosine similarity > 0.8
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each condition's pool; one value per condition. This paper says each participant submitted one idea, but Lee and Chung let Experiment 1 participants enter several ideas in one text box, about 1.69 on average (c010 PDF p. 6). Supplementary Table 1 gives n = 130 (web search) and 103 (ChatGPT) for Experiment 1, 233 in all (SI p. 3), the number of participants Lee and Chung analyzed (c010 PDF p. 6); neither document says whether an entry with several ideas was embedded whole or cut to one idea.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals for individual proportions (Fig. 1 error bars); Bonferroni-corrected confidence intervals for differences in Supplementary Table 1 (not in this PDF); the main text does not name the test, and Supplementary Table 1 uses a proportions z-test (SI p. 2)
diversity_detail.notes: Higher = more diverse; no sign reversal.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas containing the word 'sprinkler' in each condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas in each condition that include the word 'sprinkler': a keyword measure of how many people's ideas converge on one concept. A descriptive illustration in the text, with no test. Only the ChatGPT condition's denominator is printed (96 ideas).

contrasts.reported: 20 out of 96 ChatGPT-aided ideas included 'sprinkler' vs 12 in the human-only condition (number of human-only ideas not stated). A higher count means more convergence, so the sign is reversed: direction is lower diversity for ChatGPT on the printed raw counts. Shares cannot be compared without the human-only arm's size.

The arms follow Lee and Chung's Experiment 2B, which randomly assigned participants to ChatGPT-assisted or Human-only and added 100 responses that the authors obtained from ChatGPT-3.5 (c010 PDF p. 7); 'ChatGPT–human' is the ChatGPT-assisted condition, ChatGPT 'in collaboration with humans' (c010 PDF p. 3), labeled 'GPT-aided' in Supplementary Table 1 (SI p. 4). eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 met: Lee and Chung randomized participants to complete creative challenges with or without ChatGPT, against web search or no aid; this paper states it once for the series (p. 1107), and Lee and Chung state it for every experiment (c010 PDF p. 2 and Methods, pp. 6-8). Criterion 2 met: this PDF prints no people count, but for Experiment 2A it reports 96 ChatGPT-aided ideas and says each participant submitted one idea (both p. 1107), and Lee and Chung asked each Experiment 2A participant for one idea (c010 PDF p. 2), so at least 96 people were analyzed in that arm alone. The Reporting Summary's 'Data exclusions N/A' (PDF p. 5) marks the item as not applicable to a secondary analysis; it does not say that no data were excluded, and the bound does not rest on it. Supplementary Table 1 (online, not in this PDF) gives n = 291 for Experiment 2a (SI p. 3), the sample Lee and Chung analyzed after excluding 7 of 298 complete responses (c010 PDF pp. 6-7). The one-idea statement does not hold for Experiment 1 (c010 PDF p. 6), which criterion 2 does not use. Criterion 3 met: the outcome is the fraction of unique ideas among the ideas participants produced, from Universal Sentence Encoder similarity (pp. 1107-1108, Fig. 1). design_class is online_rct for all six studies: under the form-spec rule, a reanalysis takes the original experiment's design class, and Lee and Chung randomly assigned MTurk or Prolific participants in the USA in every experiment (c010 PDF pp. 6-8; c010 form). This document does not itself say where the experiments ran. The participants are Lee and Chung's (2024; candidate c010), whose analyses rated each idea individually (p. 1107); under codebook section 8 rule 4 this reanalysis can supply the across_people record for that sample. The Experiment 2b ChatGPT-only contrast compares AI output with human output and is context only.

one_line_finding: In a reanalysis of Lee and Chung's (2024) experiments, ChatGPT-aided idea pools had a lower fraction of unique ideas (Universal Sentence Encoder cosine threshold 0.8) than comparison pools in every experiment, for example 0.74 vs 0.96 with web search (Experiment 1), 0.70 vs 0.92 unaided and 0.91 with web search (Experiment 2a), and 0.41 vs 1.00 unaided (Experiment 2b); the paper reports the difference as significant in four of five experiments, all but Experiment 4 (p. 1108, Fig. 1 and text).
open_questions: Fig. 1 has six panels (1, 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 5), but the main text counts 'five experiments' and 'four out of five comparisons' without saying which Experiment 2 contrast enters the count or which cells are compared in Experiments 4 and 5. Supplementary Table 1 (online, not in this PDF) settles it: it calls the studies 'the five experiments reported in Lee & Chung' while listing 1, 2a, 2b, 3, 4 and 5; every Experiment 2 test at threshold 0.80 has p < 0.001; and Experiments 4 and 5 compare ChatGPT with web search within each level (SI pp. 2-7).

Per-condition counts of ideas and people, test statistics, and intervals are not in this PDF. Supplementary Table 1 gives the n of each condition, risk differences with 95% CIs, Cohen's h and z-tests for every contrast (SI pp. 3-8), except per-cell counts for Experiment 5, where it gives only n = 383.
Experiment 5 per-cell counts are in neither this PDF nor Supplementary Table 1; the posted data (https://osf.io/rzn87) would give them.

This document does not state the setting or population of the original experiments. Under the form-spec rule for reanalyses, design_class takes Lee and Chung's class, online_rct: they randomly assigned MTurk or Prolific participants in the USA in every experiment (c010 PDF pp. 6-8). Population and country stay as this document gives them (null, not_stated); the c010 form records them for the shared sample.

This document does not define the Experiment 2b 'ChatGPT–human' set. It is coded from Lee and Chung's Experiment 2B, whose three sets were ChatGPT-assisted participants, Human-only participants and 100 ChatGPT-3.5 responses (c010 PDF pp. 3 and 7); Supplementary Table 1 labels the set 'GPT-aided' (n = 102, SI p. 4).

This document does not describe how the second factor was set in Experiment 4 (constraints) or Experiment 5 (empathy). Lee and Chung randomly assigned each participant to one cell of a 2 x 2 between-participants design in both (c010 PDF p. 7 and pp. 7-8).
Randomization is stated once for Lee and Chung's experiments as a series, not per experiment. Lee and Chung state random assignment for every experiment (c010 PDF p. 2 and Methods, pp. 6-8).

This paper says each participant submitted one idea, but Lee and Chung's Experiment 1 participants could enter several ideas in one text box, about 1.69 on average (c010 PDF p. 6). Supplementary Table 1 gives 233 units for Experiment 1 (SI p. 3), the number of participants Lee and Chung analyzed, but neither document says whether an entry with several ideas was embedded whole or cut to one idea; the posted scripts (https://osf.io/zf3s2) would show it.

The Fig. 1 legend calls the intervals for differences in Supplementary Table 1 Bonferroni-corrected, but the table's legend says only that the p-values are corrected, and for the Experiment 4 low-constraint contrast the 95% CI [-0.125, -0.002] excludes zero while the corrected p is 0.096 (SI pp. 2 and 6). Which intervals are corrected matters for extraction, not for eligibility.
notes: Matters Arising (3 article pages) followed by the 7-page Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary. The Reporting Summary lists research sample, data exclusions, and randomization as N/A for this secondary analysis and refers ethics oversight to Lee & Chung (2024) (PDF p. 5). All Fig. 1 values were checked against the PDF text layer of p. 1108, matching each value label to its bar label by position. The paper restates Lee and Chung's finding that ChatGPT raised the average rated creativity of individual ideas (p. 1107) but reports no numbers for it, so no with_ai outcome is coded. Study ids follow form A and the reconciled c010 form (S1 = Experiment 1, S2 = 2a, S3 = 2b, S4 = 3, S5 = 4, S6 = 5); form B used S1, S2a, S2b, S3, S4, S5. Locators give journal pages (1107-1109) with PDF pages in parentheses. Finalized 2026-10-04: the seven challenge problems (assignment 4, people 2, outcome 1) were checked against this PDF, Lee and Chung (2024; c010 PDF) and the online Supplementary Information (8 pages, read from the publisher's URL; not on disk), and all seven corrections were applied. Numbers from c010 or the Supplementary Information carry 'c010 PDF p.' or 'SI p.' locators and enter no people, arm-count or contrast field. The reconciliation object is unchanged, so two of its agreed fields keep wording the final form corrects: 'one idea per participant' (wrong for Experiment 1) and 'no data exclusions' (the Reporting Summary says N/A).
